Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. In a region exhausted by conflict and the collapse of state institutions, the greatest danger is that an attempt to change Ethiopia's landlocked status by force ignites another war, at a cost to all concerned far greater than any benefit its proponents hope to gain. + / - SAVE SHARE Related topics Tigray Ethiopia Eritrea Red Sea Port international trade Horn of Africa Sudan Related Articles The leaders of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea met in Alamein Egypt on 4 October to discuss regional tensions. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia Takes Delivery of 12 Su-35 Fighter Jets, to Receive S-400 Air Defense Systems: PM Abiy 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 28, 2026 (ENA)— Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced that the country has taken delivery of its first 12 Su-35 4++ generation fighter jets and is set to receive four batteries of S-400 air defense systems. The Prime Minister described the move as a significant milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to strengthen its national defense and security capabilities. In a social media post, PM Abiy said Ethiopia’s comprehensive efforts to sustainably ensure peace and security had reached a new milestone. He added that the growing readiness of the country’s defense forces was enhancing its ability to deter potential aggression. “Today, in accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” he said, adding that Ethiopia would also receive four S-400 air defense system batteries. Prime Minister Abiy expressed gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery of the fighter jets a year ahead of the agreed schedule. He said the acquisition places Ethiopia at the forefront of Sub-Saharan African nations in equipping itself with the advanced fighter jets. The Prime Minister further elaborated that the development further strengthens Ethiopia’s sovereignty and enhances its defense capabilities, enabling the country to pursue its national security objectives while contributing to regional stability. The announcement comes as Prime Minister Abiy arrives in Moscow, Russia, to attend the Third Russia–Africa Summit, providing an opportunity to advance Ethiopia’s engagement with Russia and other African nations. The Prime Minister described the acquisition as a significant boost to Ethiopia’s collective security and its long-term efforts to safeguard national sovereignty and regional peace. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

The latest alert seems to confirm that there is still fighting in the Tigray region of Ethiopia although the regional capital Mekelle is not experiencing active fighting. In an interview with Anchor Media on Thursday, the TPLF spokesperson Dr. Abraham Hagos stated that the organization has finalized preparation for counter-offensive and is reorganized for combat in five fronts. The statement from the Embassy on Wednesday this week stated “Fighting in Tigray appears to be concentrated in areas outside Mekelle and near the border with Eritrea.” It noted that Ethiopian Airlines flights to Shire and Axum, in the Tigray region remain suspended. As was the case with the travel advisory at the beginning of this month, the U.S. Embassy advised citizens to reconsider travelling to Ethiopia and avoid traveling to Afar, Amhara and Tigray regions of Ethiopia. It also advised citizens who are already in those areas to leave if safe to do so. Also, the embassy highlighted the security situation in Moyale, a border town between Ethiopia and Kenya where there had been intense conflict earlier this week. It stated that ” The embassy also continues to monitor ongoing fighting in Moyale, the primary border with Kenya, shared by both the Oromia and Somali regions, which appears to have calmed.” However, it warned that the situation “may change at any time.” Among the actions the embassy recommended to citizens is to avoid “military installations.” Earlier this month, the U.S. disclosed military attacks targeting the capital Addis Ababa as local sources were reporting a drone attack targeting Defense Force Headquarters in the capital Addis Ababa – which Ethiopia did not confirm. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio linked the attacks to what he described as “separatists.” Notably, seven armed groups operating in the different parts of the country formed a coalition in September. It was within less than three weeks after the announcement of the coalition that the Ethiopian Defense Force launched its military operation in the Tigray region. Tigray People’s Liberation Front ( TPLF ) fighters withdrew from many towns in the region including Mekelle which they describe as “strategic retreat” However, media outlets affiliated with the government claim that the TPLF was militarily defeated and is now waging a guerilla war across Northern Tigray. On Friday, Samora Yenus, former defense chief and TPLF member, stated that the TPLF was defeated. The Maritime Security Centre–Indian Ocean (MSCIO), which supports the EU's Operation ATALANTA, said the Iranian fishing vessel Azini was reportedly hijacked at approximately 09:00 UTC on October 29. In an update displayed on October 31, MSCIO said the vessel was approaching a maritime traffic lane and could potentially be used as a mothership to support additional piracy operations. The warning does not establish that the Azini has been used to launch attacks. The safety of its crew remains unknown, and authorities have not identified those responsible for the reported hijacking. The vessel's reported movement toward a shipping traffic lane has raised concerns about possible threats to merchant ships operating off Somalia's northeastern coast. A fishing vessel used as a pirate mothership could serve as a base for attacks beyond the immediate location of the original incident, potentially exposing other vessels to additional security risks. MSCIO has not reported any confirmed attacks launched from the Azini. Shipping Operators Urged to Remain Vigilant MSCIO urged vessels operating near the reported incident to maintain heightened vigilance, follow maritime security guidance and report suspicious activity. The advisory comes as Operation ATALANTA investigates the circumstances surrounding the reported seizure. For commercial shipping operators, the immediate concern is whether the incident remains isolated or develops into a wider threat along nearby maritime routes. The potential use of the Azini as a mothership is central to the warning, although authorities have not established that the vessel is being used for piracy operations. No confirmed follow-on attacks have been identified in MSCIO's notice. advertisements Incident Reported Off Puntland Coast Puntland Post, a regional news outlet, separately reported that the incident occurred off Banderbayla on Somalia's northeastern coast. The publication also reported that two Somali guards were among those aboard the Iranian vessel. Neither detail has been independently verified, and Puntland Post did not identify the sources behind its account. MSCIO has not provided a verified account from the crew or established who carried out the reported hijacking. The available information leaves the vessel's current status, the condition of those aboard and the identity of the suspected attackers unresolved. Investigation Focuses on Potential Piracy Threat Operation ATALANTA is investigating the reported incident as maritime authorities continue to warn nearby vessels of a possible security threat. The MSCIO advisory does not establish the circumstances of the initial boarding or confirm whether the vessel is currently under the control of suspected pirates. For commercial ship operators, the next critical development will be whether authorities can establish the Azini's status and determine if the vessel poses an active threat to nearby shipping. Until then, MSCIO's guidance remains focused on heightened vigilance and reporting suspicious activity, with the risk of further pirate attacks still unconfirmed. somalia.content: Somalia Faces Rising Rift Valley Fever Risk, Threatening Livestock Livelihoods - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Faces Rising Rift Valley Fever Risk, Threatening Livestock Livelihoods Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Saturday October 31, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia faces a growing risk of Rift Valley fever that could threaten livestock-dependent livelihoods, after the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the regional bloc IGAD identified the country among six facing the highest assessed risk of the disease. The warning, issued on October 30, comes as El Niño-related rainfall creates favourable conditions for the spread of the mosquito-borne virus across Eastern Africa. FAO's October assessment identified newly suitable areas for transmission in southern Somalia and forecast a further expansion of favourable conditions across the region through January 2027. The assessment does not confirm an outbreak in Somalia. Instead, it signals an increased risk that authorities must prepare for before infections emerge or spread. The threat carries economic implications for communities that depend on livestock for their livelihoods. Rift Valley fever can cause severe illness in animals and humans, while livestock deaths and pregnancy losses can inflict significant financial damage on affected households. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the disease can cause serious illness in livestock, threatening the animals on which many rural livelihoods depend. For livestock owners, the potential losses extend beyond animals that die from infection. Pregnancy losses can also undermine the productive capacity of affected herds, increasing the economic burden of the disease. Rainfall Raises Transmission Risk Heavy rainfall is a central factor behind the latest warning. Wet conditions can expand mosquito breeding grounds, increasing the potential for transmission. Movements of livestock can also contribute to the spread of infection, making surveillance and coordination between neighbouring countries important. The FAO assessment indicates that environmental conditions suitable for transmission have emerged in additional areas of southern Somalia. It also forecasts that conditions favourable to the disease could expand across Eastern Africa through January 2027, extending the period during which authorities may need to maintain heightened surveillance. The warning places Somalia within a broader regional risk picture rather than identifying a confirmed national outbreak. Agencies Call for Early Action FAO and IGAD urged countries facing elevated risk to strengthen targeted surveillance, position vaccines and essential supplies in advance, and coordinate animal-health and public-health responses across borders. The recommended measures are intended to improve preparedness before outbreaks place additional pressure on livestock owners and health services. Cross-border coordination is particularly important because livestock movements can contribute to disease transmission, while rainfall-driven mosquito breeding conditions may affect multiple countries. The agencies' recommendations focus on detecting potential infections and ensuring that essential resources are available when needed. advertisements Human Health and Livestock Losses Rift Valley fever poses a dual threat to animal production and human health. The WHO says most human infections occur through contact with the blood or organs of infected animals. People can also become infected through bites from mosquitoes carrying the virus. No human-to-human transmission has been documented, according to the WHO. The disease's impact on animals is a major economic concern. Livestock deaths and pregnancy losses can reduce the productive value of affected herds and threaten the livelihoods of households that rely on them. Somalia has experienced Rift Valley fever during earlier periods of exceptional rainfall. The WHO records a major outbreak in 1997–98 that affected Somalia, Kenya and Tanzania following an El Niño event accompanied by extensive flooding. That history provides a precedent for the current concern, although the latest assessment identifies transmission risk rather than confirmed infections. For Somalia, the immediate priority is preparedness. The effectiveness of targeted surveillance, advance positioning of vaccines and supplies, and coordination with neighbouring countries will be critical as rainfall-related transmission conditions are forecast to persist through January 2027. Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ By Amb. Ali Mohamed Mohamud Cagabarur Saturday October 31, 2026 Lessons from 1990, the Responsibility of Today’s Intellectuals, and the Dangers of Silence at Critical Moments in a Nation’s History History is not merely a record of events that nations have experienced. It also carries lessons and warnings from which every generation must learn. A nation that fails to learn from the mistakes of its past risks confronting the same tragedies again. Somalia is a clear example of a country where the collapse of state institutions left political, social, and economic wounds from which the nation has yet to fully recover. The collapse of the central government in 1991 was not simply the end of a political system. It triggered institutional breakdown, civil war, mass displacement, and national fragmentation, the consequences of which have affected generations. Today, after decades of efforts to rebuild state institutions, Somalia is once again experiencing political disputes, constitutional disagreements, and growing mistrust among political stakeholders. Although the circumstances today differ significantly from those of 1990, history reminds us of the importance of resolving political differences before they escalate into a national crisis. This raises a question that deserves serious reflection: Where are the Somali intellectuals and respected national figures who will stand up to defend statehood, speak truth to those in power, unite the people, and prevent threats that could undermine the nation’s future? The Lesson of 1990: When Intellectuals Warned of National Collapse In late 1990, as Somalia moved closer to political and security turmoil, a group of prominent Somali intellectuals and respected national figures emerged. They included former politicians, academics, religious scholars, traditional elders, and individuals who commanded considerable respect within society. This group, widely known as the Manifesto Group, sought to play a role in preventing the impending collapse of the Somali state. They called for political reform, dialogue, and a peaceful resolution to the escalating national crisis. The historical significance of their initiative was not limited to the statement they issued. More importantly, it reflected their conviction that intellectual leadership was not merely a matter of titles, prestige, or social recognition. Rather, it carried a patriotic responsibility to speak out when the future of the nation was at risk. Although their efforts ultimately failed to prevent the collapse of the central government in 1991, they left an important historical lesson: individuals possessing knowledge, experience, and social influence have a responsibility to warn of impending dangers, facilitate dialogue, and seek solutions during periods of national crisis. The collapse of 1991 demonstrated that once public confidence, state institutions, and political leadership have been severely undermined, rebuilding them can take decades. The question facing Somalia today is therefore not merely why the state collapsed in 1991, but what lessons we have learned from that experience and what measures we are taking to prevent the repetition of past mistakes. Somalia Today: Political Disputes and the Responsibility of Intellectuals Somalia today is not Somalia of 1990. The country has government institutions, a federal political system, a constitution, and ongoing efforts to strengthen statehood. Nevertheless, the existence of these institutions alone does not guarantee political stability without public trust, accountability, and a shared national understanding of the country's future direction. Constitutional disputes, disagreements between the Federal Government and certain Federal Member States, and differing positions on the electoral process demonstrate the need for inclusive political dialogue. Statehood is not sustained by institutional authority alone. It depends on legitimacy, public confidence, respect for the constitution, and the ability of political leaders to manage disagreements while safeguarding the national interest. When political disagreements are treated as battles in which one side must defeat the other, rather than as issues requiring dialogue and compromise, achieving sustainable solutions becomes increasingly difficult. This is precisely where the responsibility of Somali intellectuals begins. Every society has individuals who may not hold public office but possess knowledge, experience, credibility, and the ability to influence public opinion and political decision-making. Such individuals can serve as bridges between opposing parties, independent voices willing to speak the truth, and constructive forces working to protect the national interest. However, they cannot fulfill this responsibility if they become absorbed in political rivalries, align themselves with competing factions, or remain silent on matters of national importance to protect personal relationships and private interests. True intellectual leadership does not mean agreeing with everything those in power do. It means having the courage to tell them the truth, even when that truth is uncomfortable or unwelcome. The Silence of Intellectuals: A Responsibility That Cannot Be Evaded There is a fundamental difference between neutrality and silence. Neutrality means remaining independent of competing political interests and assessing events according to fairness, evidence, and conscience. Silence, however, when motivated by fear, personal interests, or a desire to please those in power, can amount to an abandonment of one's responsibility to society. Somali intellectuals must be able to engage equally with government leaders, opposition figures, and all political stakeholders. They must speak openly about political mistakes without directing criticism exclusively at one side or defending those with whom they share personal or political interests. Religious scholars, academics, former political leaders, diplomats, businesspeople, traditional elders, women, and young Somalis all share a responsibility to protect social cohesion and the continuity of Somali statehood. Former political leaders and experienced diplomats, in particular, should draw upon the lessons they have learned from leadership, political negotiations, and conflict resolution. Their experience should serve the national interest rather than being confined to commentary and observation. Somalia does not need intellectuals who automatically align themselves with those currently in power or those seeking to replace them. It needs independent national voices whose commitment to the country transcends temporary political interests. A nation cannot be saved through applause and unquestioning praise. It is safeguarded through sincere advice, truthfulness, national unity, and leadership that accepts accountability. The Urgent Need for a National Gathering One of the most important lessons from the efforts of Somali intellectuals in 1990 is that political disputes should not be allowed to deteriorate to the point where peaceful resolution becomes increasingly difficult. Somali intellectuals should initiate independent national consultations to address the country's political situation, constitutional disagreements, electoral processes, and the restoration of confidence in national institutions. Such consultations should remain independent of the Federal Government, Federal Member States, and opposition groups. They should bring together respected individuals known for their integrity, knowledge, impartiality, and experience. The objective should not be to establish another political organization or create a competing center of authority. Rather, it should be to develop a unified civic voice, formulate practical recommendations, and facilitate mediation among political stakeholders. Intellectuals should encourage all parties to resolve constitutional disputes through lawful procedures and dialogue, pursue an electoral process grounded in broad political agreement, and ensure that public authority is exercised in the national interest. Equally important is the need to warn against the exploitation of clan divisions, public incitement, and inflammatory political rhetoric that could intensify tensions. A country that has endured decades of civil conflict and fragmentation needs political leadership willing to compromise and a society capable of preventing political disagreements from escalating into violence. Government and Opposition: A Shared National Responsibility The responsibility to protect Somali statehood does not rest exclusively with those currently in office, nor does it belong solely to the opposition. It is a shared obligation among political stakeholders and society as a whole. Every government has a duty to uphold the constitution, strengthen national institutions, protect citizens' rights, and resolve political disagreements through dialogue and mutual understanding. Similarly, the opposition has a responsibility to present constructive political alternatives, preserve peace, and avoid actions that could undermine the continuity of state institutions. Political disagreement is a natural and legitimate feature of democracy. What matters is ensuring that such disagreements do not destroy the institutions and constitutional principles within which all political actors must operate. Those who hold public office today must recognize that political authority is temporary, while statehood is a national inheritance belonging to both present and future generations. The Somali state must always be greater than the individual who leads it, the political party that governs it, or any group seeking to control it. Conclusion: Let Us Not Become Silent Spectators Whom History Will Hold Accountable Somalia has paid an extraordinarily high price for the collapse of its state institutions. Thousands of families lost loved ones, while millions of Somalis experienced displacement, exile, and hardship as a result of civil conflict and institutional breakdown. Generations of Somalis have grown up without adequate public services, reliable security, or sufficient economic opportunities to build their futures. Today, our generation carries a historic responsibility to protect what has been rebuilt and prevent mistakes that could undermine decades of state-building efforts. The intellectuals of 1990 attempted to warn the nation of the dangers it faced. Today, more than fourteen years after the establishment of the non-transitional Federal Government in 2012, a critical question must be asked: Who will assume the responsibility of bringing national voices together, reducing political tensions, and safeguarding the future of Somali statehood? The time has come for Somali intellectuals to move beyond isolated statements, media commentary, and political alignments toward meaningful consultations and a collective effort to identify national solutions. History remembers more than the leaders who held political power. It also remembers those who demonstrated the courage to defend the public interest, those who worked to prevent national tragedies, and those who remained silent when their country needed them most. Somali statehood is a national inheritance achieved through decades of struggle and immense sacrifice. It is not the property of any particular government, political party, or group in power. It is a collective responsibility belonging to the entire Somali people. The question, therefore, remains: Where are the Somali intellectuals and respected national figures who will stand up today to safeguard Somalia's future? Somalia must not wait for another national catastrophe to recognize the value of statehood. What the country needs is an awakened national conscience, leadership willing to accept constructive advice, and intellectuals with the courage to speak the truth. A nation must be saved while there is still an opportunity to correct its course—not after its collapse has become an irreversible reality. Writer: Amb. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice we are handing over security to our Somali brothers,” Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, chief of Uganda’s defense forces, wrote on X. advertisements Ugandan authorities have not publicly announced how many troops are leaving, which bases will be handed over first or when the withdrawal will be completed. Uganda remains the largest troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia, or AUSSOM. The African Union authorized 4,500 Ugandan troops for the mission, which replaced the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia at the start of 2025. AUSSOM’s mandate includes supporting Somali forces against al-Shabab, protecting civilians and key infrastructure, and gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somali security institutions. The mission’s current transition plan envisages a phased drawdown toward a final exit by December 2029, subject to security conditions. Uganda first deployed troops to Somalia in March 2007 as the lead contingent in the African Union Mission in Somalia, or AMISOM, becoming one of the longest-serving foreign military contributors to the country’s security operations. Ugandan forces have since fought in some of the most significant battles against al-Shabab and have operated across Mogadishu and large parts of Lower Shabelle. The deployment has also come at a heavy cost. Ugandan troops have suffered repeated casualties in al-Shabab attacks, including major assaults on African Union bases over the course of the mission. The announcement comes as AUSSOM faces persistent funding shortages. The African Union Peace and Security Council has repeatedly warned that inadequate and unpredictable financing threatens the mission’s operations and has called for additional international support. The AU has also emphasized that decisions over AUSSOM’s future and troop withdrawals should be based on assessments of conditions on the ground and coordinated with Somalia to avoid creating security gaps. Uganda has remained a central part of that security architecture. Earlier this year, the African Union praised Kampala for deploying additional troops to Somalia on a bilateral basis as a temporary response to deteriorating security conditions. Al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, continues to control or operate across parts of rural southern and central Somalia despite nearly two decades of military pressure from Somali forces and their international partners. Kainerugaba’s announcement therefore represents a significant shift in Uganda’s long-running role in Somalia, but it remains unclear whether the move marks the beginning of a full national withdrawal or a phased reduction coordinated with AUSSOM and Somali authorities. Share Somalia had requested an end to UN's longstanding political mission in the country. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia formally ended its operations on Saturday, concluding a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN political engagement in the Horn of Africa country. The closure of the mission, known as UNTMIS, came at the request of the Somali government, according to a statement issued by the mission. The UN said successive political missions had supported Somalia through critical stages of peacebuilding and state-building, helping Somali-led efforts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and promote national reconciliation. "Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia — rather, it marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another," said Raisedon Zenenga, the mission's officer-in-charge and deputy special representative of the UN secretary-general for Somalia. UN says it is still committed to long-lasting peace efforts in Somalia The UN said it would remain committed to Somalia through its resident agencies and broader presence in the country, supporting efforts toward peace, stability, sustainable development and prosperity. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres commended the determination and resilience of the Somali people despite the challenges facing the country. Hassan Sheikh's latest remarks reinforce Mogadishu's stated position of avoiding involvement in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute while maintaining working relationships with both governments. “Somalia would continue prioritizing peaceful relations and cooperation as part of broader efforts to promote stability in the Horn of Africa,” he added. استبدل صلاح بعد مرور 60 دقيقة من مباراة أنغولا ضمن تصفيات كأس أمم أفريقيا 2027، وقال في المؤتمر الصحافي عقب اللقاء إن القرار جاء «لأسباب فنية». وبعدها غادر صلاح المعسكر، وغاب عن المباراة التالية أمام جنوب السودان، وهو ما أوضح مدرب المنتخب أنه تم بالاتفاق مع اللاعب بسبب إقامة المباراة على أرضية من العشب الصناعي حفاظاً على سلامته. كما غاب مهاجم طرابزون سبور عن المباراة الودية أمام جنوب أفريقيا لاحقاً، وسط تساؤلات عديدة بشأن موقفه من الانضمام إلى المعسكر المقبل في نوفمبر. وسعى حسن بعد ذلك إلى احتواء التوتر، مؤكداً احترامه لجميع اللاعبين، وفي مقدمتهم قائد المنتخب صلاح، الذي وصفه بأنه «من أهم اللاعبين في العالم». ويستعد منتخب مصر لخوض مواجهتي مالاوي ضمن الجولتين الثالثة والرابعة من التصفيات المؤهلة إلى كأس أمم أفريقيا 2027، حيث ينطلق المعسكر في التاسع من نوفمبر بمركز المنتخبات الوطنية. ومن المقرر أن يلتقي المنتخبان يوم 13 نوفمبر على استاد القاهرة الدولي ضمن منافسات الجولة الثالثة، قبل أن تتجدد المواجهة بينهما يوم 17 من الشهر نفسه في مالاوي ضمن الجولة الرابعة. ويتصدر منتخب مصر المجموعة الثانية برصيد 4 نقاط، متفوقاً بفارق الأهداف على أنغولا صاحبة المركز الثاني، بينما تحتل مالاوي المركز الثالث برصيد 3 نقاط، ويقبع منتخب جنوب السودان في المركز الأخير دون رصيد. وكان المنتخب المصري قد استهل مشواره بالتعادل السلبي أمام أنغولا في القاهرة، قبل أن يحقق فوزاً كبيراً على جنوب السودان خارج أرضه بخمسة أهداف دون رد. وقال الاتحاد المصري إن إبراهيم حاجي عثمان أوغلو، رئيس الاتحاد التركي، استقبل أبو ريدة «في إطار تعزيز العلاقات الثنائية وتطوير أوجه التعاون المشترك بين الاتحادين المصري والتركي». وأضاف أن اللقاء «تناول بحث سبل تعزيز التعاون في مختلف المجالات الكروية، وتبادل الخبرات الفنية والإدارية، وتطوير برامج إعداد المنتخبات الوطنية، إلى جانب التعاون في مجالات التحكيم وتطوير المواهب والبنية المؤسسية لكرة القدم. وشهد اللقاء الاتفاق على إعداد بروتوكول تعاون مشترك بين الاتحادين المصري والتركي، يتضمن تبادل إقامة المعسكرات التدريبية للمنتخبات الوطنية للشباب والناشئين ومنتخبات كرة القدم النسائية، إلى جانب تبادل الخبرات وتنظيم برامج مشتركة لتطوير منظومة التحكيم، بما يتيح الاستفادة من الإمكانات والخبرات المتاحة لدى الجانبين». وقال الاتحاد إن الزيارة ستتضمن أيضاً «حضور إحدى مباريات الدوري التركي لكرة القدم لنادي طرابزون سبور، الذي يضم بين صفوفه قائد منتخب مصر صلاح». football.summary: كشف الاتحاد الأفريقي لكرة القدم «كاف» عن مواعيد مباريات الأندية المصرية الزمالك وبيراميدز والأهلي في بطولتي دوري أبطال أفريقيا والكونفدرالية لموسم 2026/2027. حيث سيتنافس الزمالك وبيراميدز في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، بينما يشارك الأهلي في الكونفدرالية. تم تقسيم الفرق إلى أربع مجموعات، حيث وقع الزمالك في المجموعة الثانية مع يانج أفريكانز التنزاني، مولودية الجزائر، والنادي الأفريقي التونسي. تبدأ مباريات الزمالك في الجولة الأولى بمواجهة الأفريقي التونسي في نهاية نوفمبر 2026. من جهة أخرى، يلعب بيراميدز في المجموعة الرابعة مع الهلال السوداني، حوريا الغيني، والمغرب الفاسي، حيث يواجه المغرب الفاسي في الجولة الأولى. أما الأهلي، فقد وقع في المجموعة الأولى مع الرجاء المغربي، أول أغسطس الأنجولي، وإسكو كارا التوجولي، حيث يبدأ مبارياته بمواجهة أول أغسطس. ستنطلق المنافسات في نوفمبر 2026.

football.title: خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق - تاق برس
football.content: خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق — تاق برس اعجاب المتابعين الأحد, نوفمبر 1, 2026 من نحن السياسة التحريرية للإعلان على تاق برس اتصل بنا تاق برس - اخبار السودان والعالم الرئيسية أخبار عاجلة سياسية منوعات وثقافة إقتصاد رياضة علوم وتكنلوجيا مقالات أخري تقارير صحة الرئيسية أخبار رياضة خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق خلافات تهدد مشروع أبياه مع المنتخب السوداني.. والرحيل يلوح في الأفق بواسطة editor في أكتوبر 31, 2026 140 مشاركة متابعات تاق برس – تتجه العلاقة بين الغاني كواسي أبياه، المدير الفني للمنتخب الوطني السوداني الأول، والاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم نحو منعطف بالغ الخطورة، في ظل تصاعد الضغوط والتدخلات التي باتت تحاصر المدرب، وتضع تجربته مع صقور الجديان على المحك، وسط مؤشرات متزايدة على اقتراب نهاية مشواره مع المنتخب. وتشير المعلومات التي تحصل عليها “الترا سودان” من داخل مجلس إدارة الاتحاد إلى أن أبياه بات يشعر بأن ما يتعرض له يمثل تحركات منظمة تستهدف تقويض صلاحياته وإضعاف موقفه، تمهيداً لإبعاده عن قيادة المنتخب. وهو ما أسرّ به لعدد من المقربين منه، معبّراً عن استيائه الشديد من الأجواء التي يعمل فيها. وبحسب المعلومات ذاتها، فإن المدرب الغاني بات يعتقد أن هناك مخططاً يُحاك ضده، وأن بعض القرارات والتوجهات الأخيرة داخل الاتحاد لا يمكن فصلها عن مساعٍ لإجباره على مغادرة موقعه، بعدما وجد نفسه في مواجهة تدخلات متكررة في صميم اختصاصاته الفنية. التغييرات التي طالت الجهازين الإداري والفني المساعد لم تكن أمراً عابراً بالنسبة للمدرب الغاني، خصوصاً بعد إبعاد المدير الإداري أبوبكر الماحي، وابتعاد المدرب العام صلاح الفنج عن موقعه ضمن المنظومة التي عملت معه خلال الفترة الماضية. ويمثل الرجلان عنصرين مهمين في منظومة أبياه، وكان المدرب ينظر إليهما باعتبارهما من ركائز الاستقرار داخل المنتخب، الأمر الذي دفعه إلى المطالبة بإعادة ترتيب الأوضاع بما يضمن عودة الانسجام إلى الجهازين الفني والإداري. لكن ما حدث عزز شعوره بأن هناك توجهاً لإعادة تشكيل المنظومة المحيطة به، دون اعتبار لرؤيته أو احتياجاته، وبكوادر لا تمتلك بالضرورة الخبرة المطلوبة للعمل في منتخب بحجم صقور الجديان. ومن أكثر الملفات التي أثارت غضب أبياه الضغوط المتواصلة بشأن إبعاد عدد من أصحاب الخبرة والعناصر الأساسية التي شكلت العمود الفقري للمنتخب خلال مشواره الأخير. فالمدرب الغاني لا يرى مبرراً للتخلي عن عناصر أثبتت جدارتها وقدمت الكثير للمنتخب، لمجرد ارتباط بعضها بملف المطالبة بالمستحقات المالية. كما لا يخفي تحفظاته على محاولات فرض أسماء جديدة ضمن القائمة، دون أن تكون هناك قناعة فنية مكتملة بشأن قدراتها. وتفاقمت الأزمة مع التوجه نحو تغيير نسبة من قوام المنتخب وإقحام عناصر من منتخب الشباب، في وقت يرى فيه أبياه أن الإحلال والتجديد لا ينبغي أن يتحولا إلى قرارات فوقية تتجاوز التقييم الفني واحتياجات المنتخب. ولم تتوقف مصادر الإحباط عند التدخل في اختيار اللاعبين وإدارة الجهاز الفني، بل امتدت إلى عدم تنفيذ عدد من البرامج الإعدادية التي اقترحها المدرب، وفي مقدمتها إقامة معسكر مبكر عقب فراغ الهلال والمريخ من مشاركتهما في البطولات الأفريقية. وكان أبياه يعوّل على الاستفادة من تلك الفترة في تجهيز المنتخب بصورة مثالية، والاستفادة من وجود العناصر الأساسية في السودان. غير أن عدم الاستجابة للمقترح أضاف حلقة جديدة إلى سلسلة الخلافات بينه والاتحاد. وبدا للمدرب أن برامجه وتصوراته لا تجد الاهتمام المطلوب، وأنه مطالب بتحقيق النتائج وتحمل المسؤولية كاملة، دون أن تتوفر له الظروف والصلاحيات اللازمة. التطور الأكثر إثارة في هذه الأزمة أن أبياه، وفقاً للمعلومات التي تحصلت عليها مصادرنا، لمح للمقربين منه بأن مواجهتي المنتخب أمام السنغال ذهاباً وإياباً قد تكونان آخر مشاويره مع صقور الجديان. وتشير هذه المعطيات إلى أن المدرب الغاني بدأ بالفعل التفكير في وضع حد لتجربته عقب المباراتين، في ظل قناعته بأن الأجواء الحالية لم تعد تساعده على مواصلة العمل بالصورة التي يريدها، وأن حجم التدخلات والضغوط تجاوز الحدود التي يمكن التعايش معها. وإذا مضى أبياه في هذا الاتجاه، فإن المنتخب الوطني سيكون أمام خسارة مدرب كبير قاده إلى مرحلة مميزة من النتائج والإنجازات، في وقت يحتاج فيه إلى الاستقرار والاستمرارية أكثر من حاجته إلى الدخول في مغامرة فنية وإدارية جديدة. ما يحدث الآن يتجاوز خلافاً حول قائمة أو لاعب أو معسكر إعدادي. نحن أمام أزمة ثقة تتسع يوماً بعد يوم، ومدرب بات يشعر بأنه مستهدف، وأن هناك من يعمل على إضعاف تجربته وإفقاده أدوات النجاح، قبل أن يصبح رحيله أمراً واقعاً. والسؤال الذي ينبغي أن يجيب عنه الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم ليس ما إذا كان أبياه سيغادر فحسب، بل من يتحمل مسؤولية الوصول بعلاقة المنتخب مع مدرب صنع معه إنجازات كبيرة إلى هذه المرحلة؟ هل هناك مشروع فني بديل يستحق التضحية بتجربة أبياه؟ أم أن صقور الجديان يدفعون ثمن صراعات وتدخلات إدارية لا علاقة لها بمصلحة المنتخب؟ المؤكد أن خسارة أبياه، إن حدثت بالطريقة التي تلوح في الأفق، ستكون بداية هدم مشروع كان يستحق الحماية والاستقرار والبناء عليه. اتحاد كرة القدم صقور الجديان كواسي أبياه 140 مشاركة أخبار ذات صلة رياضة أبياه يعلن القائمة الأولية لصقور
